model_chosen.storage: A separate table, email_change_requests (migration 0129, append-only, with its .down.sql): id, user_id, new_email, token_hash, expires_at, used_at, created_at, a UNIQUE index on token_hash and an index on user_id. Mirrors password_reset_tokens (0012) and email_verification_tokens (0013).
model_chosen.why_not_columns_on_users: The lifecycle a pending change needs — issued / used / expired / superseded — is exactly the lifecycle those two tables already have; the hot users row stays untouched by a flow that may never complete; and ON DELETE CASCADE disposes of pending requests with the account (proven against real PostgreSQL).
model_chosen.token: 256 bits of entropy, delivered ONCE to the NEW address; only its hex SHA-256 is persisted. SHA-256 rather than bcrypt because the token is already random. TTL 1 hour — the password-reset window, not the 24h verification one: the user is in their settings when they ask, so an hour is ample and the window in which a stolen mailbox link is worth anything is as small as it can be.
model_chosen.atomicity: ConfirmEmailChange is ONE statement. A CTE consumes the token (its predicate includes token_hash, user_id, used_at IS NULL and expires_at > now()) and the outer UPDATE users moves the address and sets email_verified from the CTE's returned row. No transaction is needed, two concurrent confirmations cannot both win, and there is no window in which the token is spent and the address is not.
model_chosen.indistinctness: Unknown, already used, expired, or issued to ANOTHER account all match nothing, return no row, and answer 400 — one answer, so a caller cannot probe which.
model_chosen.pending_state: GET /api/v1/auth/me/email-change always answers 200: {pending:false} or {pending:true, new_email, requested_at, expires_at}. It never carries the token. An EXPIRED request does not read as pending (the read filters on expires_at itself).

shipped_rules_as_shipped.request: POST /api/v1/auth/me/email-change {current_password, new_email} -> 202 with the pending state. Re-verifies the CURRENT password; the live users.email is untouched; a single-use expiring token is mailed to the NEW address. A second request supersedes the first (the previous unused row is deleted BEFORE the new one is written, never the other way round).
shipped_rules_as_shipped.confirm: POST /api/v1/auth/me/email-change/confirm {token} -> 200 {email}. Behind requireAuth as well as the token: the mail token proves the mailbox, the session proves whose account it is. Sets email_verified TRUE in the same statement — consuming a token delivered to the address IS the possession proof, so an account can never hold an address it has not verified.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.resend: POST /api/v1/auth/me/email-change/resend -> 202, superseding the token. Takes NO body and does not re-ask for the password: the pending row is itself the record that the password was proven, and the message can only ever go to the address that request already named. 404 when nothing is pending.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.cancel: DELETE /api/v1/auth/me/email-change -> 204, killing the token. 404 when nothing was pending, rather than reporting success for a no-op.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.wrong_password: 403 'incorrect password', with the stored hash byte-identical afterwards and nothing pending.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.passwordless_accounts: 409 with 'this account has no password: use the password reset flow to set one' — the same rule the password slice set, and for the same reason: bcrypt can never verify an empty hash, so no supplied password could satisfy it and a 403 would be unfalsifiable.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.address_already_in_use: 409 'that email address is already in use on this instance' when the address resolves to ANOTHER account's SIGN-IN identifier — its email OR its username. The username half matters because sign-in accepts both with EMAIL TAKING PRECEDENCE, so an address equal to somebody's username would silently shadow their sign-in, and usernames predating the '@' ban may literally be addresses.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.own_username_is_allowed: An address equal to the CALLER'S OWN username is ACCEPTED: it shadows nobody, and a legacy account whose username IS an address must be able to set it. This is the deliberate other half of the collision rule.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.disclosure_rule: Refusing a taken address discloses exactly what registration already discloses: registration answers 409 'username or email already taken' today, anonymously. So an authenticated caller learns nothing here that an anonymous one cannot already learn, and the wording is a single sentence for both the email and the username case (the audit reason distinguishes them).
shipped_rules_as_shipped.same_address: 422 'that is already the address on this account', case-insensitively.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.malformed: 422, by the same looksLikeEmail rule registration uses.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.anonymous: 401 on all five routes, including the confirmation.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.rate_limit: The request, the resend and the confirmation are behind the SAME strict auth limiter as login and the password change, which runs BEFORE requireAuth. The pending-state READ and the CANCEL deliberately are not: a settings page load must not be able to exhaust a budget shared with sign-in.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.sessions: NOT revoked. An email address is not a credential — knowing it grants nothing — and the change is already gated on the password, so signing every device out would be a cost with no security bought. Nothing here stamps revoked_reason because nothing here signs anything out. The old-address notice is the safeguard instead.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.mail_confirmation: To the NEW address and nowhere else. NOT best-effort: a pending request whose message never left is a dead end the user cannot see, so a failed send fails the request and leaves the address alone.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.mail_notice: To the OLD address, best-effort (the address has already moved; reporting a failure would read as 'your address did not change'), and it NAMES the new address — it is the last message that mailbox will ever get, and its reader needs to know what happened and be able to prove it to an operator. No token, no link that could change anything.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.audit: auth.email_change.request / .confirm / .cancel, success and failure with a reason naming the RULE (invalid_password, password_not_set, email_unchanged, email_taken, invalid_token). NEITHER ADDRESS appears in any event — the sensitive-key discipline keeps email out of the audit trail, asserted by scanning the whole captured log.

SC1_two_step_flow.assertions: roughly half of the 114, across the SC1 and SC1b phases, 0 failed
SC1_two_step_flow.request_changes_nothing: 202 with the pending state; the DB's users.email is unchanged and /auth/me still reads the old address; the pending state is readable; exactly one pending row exists and its stored key is the SHA-256 of the delivered token, not the token.
SC1_two_step_flow.delivery: Exactly one message, to the NEW address, over real SMTP from the configured SMTP_FROM, subject naming the instance, carrying NO password and saying in words that the account keeps its current address until the code is used. NOTHING was sent to the old address at this step.
SC1_two_step_flow.confirm: 200 returning the new address; the DB shows the address moved and email_verified TRUE; the password hash is untouched; the pending state is cleared; the OLD address receives the notice, which names the new address and carries no token; the new address gets no second message.
SC1_two_step_flow.supersede: A second request issues a different token and kills the first: the superseded token is 400 and moves nothing, and the pending state names the newest address.
SC1_two_step_flow.resend: 202, keeps the pending address, issues a NEW token, and the pre-resend token is dead.
SC1_two_step_flow.expiry: With the row aged past its window, the request no longer reads as pending and its token is 400 — and moves nothing.
SC1_two_step_flow.cancel: 204 (and it sweeps the dead rows too), then 404 for a second cancel and for a resend with nothing pending; a cancelled token is 400.
SC1_two_step_flow.rate_limit: PROVEN on the route itself: an unpaced burst of 14 wrong-password requests answered 403 x8 then 429 x6, on the shipped 10/min per-IP auth limiter, which was never raised.

SC2_refusals.assertions: every refusal is followed by an independent DB read of the address, a pending-count read, and a mail-sink read; 0 failed
SC2_refusals.wrong_password: 403, hash byte-identical, counted by the limiter (the burst above is the proof).
SC2_refusals.passwordless: 409 whose body points at the reset flow; the empty hash is still empty afterwards.
SC2_refusals.another_accounts_username: 409 — bob asking for carol's username-shaped login is refused.
SC2_refusals.own_username: 202 — stated as its own assertion, because it is the deliberate other half of the rule.
SC2_refusals.malformed_and_missing: 422 for a malformed address and for a missing current_password.
SC2_refusals.anonymous: 401 on POST, GET, DELETE, resend and confirm.
SC2_refusals.another_users_token: 400, alice's address unmoved, bob's address unmoved, AND the refused attempt did not consume the token (alice's own confirmation still worked afterwards).
SC2_refusals.no_side_effects: The whole refusal phase sent ZERO messages to the sink.

SC3_consequences.login_moved: Login with the OLD address is 401; with the NEW address 200.
SC3_consequences.me: /auth/me shows the new address and email_verified true; so does the settings UI after a hard reload.
SC3_consequences.password_reset_follows_the_address: A reset requested for the NEW address is delivered there and NOT to the old one; a reset requested for the OLD address is still 202 (enumeration-safe) and delivers nothing.
SC3_consequences.sessions_not_revoked: A second session opened before the change keeps working afterwards, and the database shows ZERO revoked session rows for the account. Recorded as the shipped decision with its reasoning, not as an oversight.
SC3_consequences.revoked_reason: Not written by this flow, because this flow signs nothing out.

SC4_ui.where: components/auth/ChangeEmailSection.tsx, mounted in SecuritySettingsView ABOVE the Password card — the address is the more consequential of the two and both are gated on the same current-password proof. A NAMED region, because with two-factor on the page now carries three correctly-labelled 'Current password' inputs.
SC4_ui.states: Current address; then either the form (new address + current password, submit disabled until both are filled) or the PENDING state naming the address with Resend and Cancel — the way out of 'we mailed a link to an address you cannot read'.
SC4_ui.errors: Through the shared Alert (role=alert): 403 'That is not your current password.', and the TWO 409s as different sentences — an address already in use, versus an account that signs in without a password, which links to /reset-password. Success is Alert variant=success (role=status).
SC4_ui.landing_route: app/email-change/confirm/page.tsx + components/auth/ConfirmEmailChangeForm.tsx, mirroring /verify-email/confirm and /reset-password/confirm. One difference: this endpoint needs the SESSION too, so a signed-out reader is asked to sign in and the token STAYS in the URL rather than being spent on a request with no bearer token; it also waits for the boot-time session restore before submitting.

harness_made_the_collision_actor_its_own.symptom: 'another account's USERNAME is 409: got 202' plus two consequential failures

harness_made_the_collision_actor_its_own.outcome: The code was right; the RULE was under-stated. Both halves are now separate assertions — another account's username is 409, the caller's own username is 202 — and the reasoning (an address equal to your own username shadows nobody, and a legacy account whose username IS an address must be able to set it) is now written down rather than implied.

existing_test_caught_the_new_mount.outcome: That test mocks @/lib/api method by method, so a new card that reads its pending state on mount breaks it. The mock gained the stub; NO assertion was weakened.

delete_unused_sweeps_expired_rows_too.found_by: the real-PostgreSQL test, which expected 2 deletions and got 3
delete_unused_sweeps_expired_rows_too.outcome: The assumption was mine, not a bug: 'unused' is used_at IS NULL and says nothing about expiry, so a superseding request tidies up every dead row it owns. That is why the pending READ filters on expires_at itself instead of trusting the table to hold only live rows. The test now asserts 3 and says why.

attempts_and_corrections: The lab's own bootstrap was wrong twice: the owner-claim response's token field is `token`, not `access_token`, and a DROP DATABASE issued while the previous API process still held connections silently failed, so a 'fresh' run started on the old data and found no first-run token. Both are harness bugs; the driver now resets the database with the API stopped.

The auth limiter is 10/min per IP and shared across register / login / reset / password change / and now the three email-change writes, so the driver paces itself to 9 per rolling 60s and only stops pacing inside the limiter phase, which is its assertion. The limit was never raised.

The GENERAL 120/min limiter ended two back-to-back browser runs: a settings page load costs about ten calls, and three walkthroughs in a couple of minutes exceed the budget. The runs were paced apart instead of raising the limit; two complete walkthroughs then passed clean.
The first browser attempt at the replay case waited on a locator that had already settled differently; it now settles and reads the page text, which is stable across both runs.

Two unit-test mutations were run to prove the new tests are load-bearing rather than merely green: swapping the sign-in lookup for a plain email lookup turns the username-collision case red, and removing the supersede-delete turns the superseded-token case red. Both restored.
browser_walkthrough: Signed up through the real form as a fresh actor and reached /settings/security.
The Email card is present and shows the current address.
Requesting the change shows the pending state naming the NEW address, with Cancel offered.
A HARD RELOAD keeps the pending state (it is server state) and the card still shows the OLD address.
The confirmation arrived at the new address over real SMTP and carried a token.
A WRONG token lands on an explicit failure, claims no success, and changes nothing.
The real token's landing page states the new address.
A hard reload of /settings/security shows the NEW address, not the old one, with the form back (nothing pending).
The OLD mailbox has the notice, and it names the new address.
Replaying the consumed link is refused.
In a separate context: the OLD address no longer signs in, the NEW one does.
In another context: a signed-out reader is asked to sign in rather than having the token spent.
findings_recorded_not_fixed: On an instance with NO working SMTP an email change cannot be completed at all: the confirmation IS the flow, so it fails closed rather than silently. That is the safe direction, but it means the AUTH-03 / A05 SMTP-selection gate now governs one more capability.

There is still no in-app notification type for account-security events (internal/notification's vocabulary is follow / comment / comment_reply / message / report_resolved / video_rejected / caption_ready / new_video / new_report), so the password-change and email-change notices are email-only. Adding a type is a product decision plus a prefs-registry row.

The auth limiter is keyed per IP and SHARED across register / login / reset / password change / email change. This slice adds three more routes to that bucket, which makes the standing finding — behind a proxy that does not set a trusted client IP, one user can exhaust everyone's budget — the most consequential of the open A12 rulings.

The admin surface still cannot move an address: PATCH /admin/users/{id} 422s an email and can only toggle email_verified. An operator helping a user who has lost BOTH their password and their mailbox therefore has no supported path. Deliberately out of scope here (self-service was the clause), but it is the obvious next question.
The .next/standalone chunk-404 finding from the profile slice was NOT re-tested — this walkthrough used `next start` against the production build, as the last two did — so it remains open.
open_product_rulings_carried_forward: Whether an admin may 'Reactivate' a tombstoned row.
The 10/min auth limiter being keyed per IP and shared, behind proxies that do not set a trusted client IP.
Mention notifications, which are not a shipped capability.
a12_stopping_criterion: MET. Every clause of the AUTH-05 procedure has live evidence: profile/privacy and the account archive (a12-profile-archive), deactivation and deletion with content, DM retention, media cleanup and the search hook (a12-deletion), password change with re-verification on session-bound access tokens (a12-password-change), and email change with re-verification (a12-email-change). The row flips to PASS (candidate; unmerged) — candidate because nothing is merged and nothing is deployed. The open rulings above are follow-ups, not blockers, and none is a gap in what the row asserts.
